system_message:
You are generating a synthetic but clinically grounded
conversation for exactly one hospital admission.

Rules:
1. Use only facts supported by the provided admission context.
2. The discharge notes are the backbone of the hospital-course
   narrative. Use them first.
3. The ordered problem list should shape the main clinical focus.
4. Radiology, procedures, microbiology, and the previous-admission
   summary are supporting context, not a checklist.
5. Not every packet item needs to appear in the conversation.
6. Speakers must be exactly: Doctor and Patient.
7. Every conversation line must contain:
   - turn number
   - exact timestamp
   - speaker
   - text
8. Timestamps must be monotonically increasing and stay within the
   admission start and admission end times.
9. Keep the conversation medically plausible and understandable to
   a patient.
10. Use short natural exchanges, patient questions, clarifications,
    explanations, reassurance, and follow-up discussion.
11. Do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, test findings,
    or outcomes.
12. Do not mention the dataset, packet, note types, or that the
    conversation is synthetic.
13. Generate the conversation first, then write the summary strictly from the generated conversation_lines.
14. Every claim in summary.summary_paragraph and every item in summary.problems must be explicitly supported by the conversation_lines.
15. Return output that exactly matches the required JSON schema.
task_message:
Generate one rich patient-doctor conversation for this admission and one admission summary.

Generation guidance:
- Approximate stay length: 6 day(s).
- Recommended turn range: 50-70 turns.
- Exact admission window: 2181-09-06 12:04:00 to 2181-09-11 15:55:00.
- Focus first on the discharge-note storyline and the core admission problems.
- Use radiology, procedures, and microbiology only as supporting detail when they help the story.
- Do not try to mention every packet item.
- Let the conversation unfold across admission, mid-course updates, and discharge planning.
- Prefer many short natural exchanges over a few long summary turns.
- The patient should ask questions, express concerns, seek clarification, and respond to updates throughout the stay.
- The doctor should explain results, treatment changes, progress, and follow-up in multiple conversational beats over time.
- You may paraphrase and add natural conversational glue, but do not invent unsupported diagnoses, procedures, findings, or outcomes.
- Generate the conversation first, then derive the final summary only from the conversation_lines you wrote.
- The final summary must contain admission start time, admission end time, one paragraph summary, and a list of problems.
- Final self-check before returning JSON: turn_number contiguous from 1; conversation_lines.time nondecreasing and inside the exact admission window; summary.admission_start and summary.admission_end copied exactly from the packet; no conversation line has empty text.

previous_admission_summary_used.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of liver transplant, chronic kidney disease, and GERD was admitted for fevers and myalgias. He presented with a temperature of 101°F and diffuse muscle pain, likely due to an influenza-like illness. Given his immunosuppressed state, he was started on empiric Tamiflu. Initial labs showed elevated liver enzymes, which persisted despite resolution of fever. Blood and urine cultures were negative, and imaging showed no acute findings. A liver biopsy revealed mild acute cellular rejection, prompting an increase in sirolimus from 2 mg to 3 mg daily. His symptoms resolved, and he was discharged home with plans for follow-up labs, an MRCP, and hepatitis B vaccination. During admission, he was also diagnosed with type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.7%) and advised on dietary management.
problems: Diabetes mellitus without mention of complication, type II or unspecified type, not stated as uncontrolled

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Patel. I understand you came in because of chills and some abnormal lab results?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. I had chills yesterday, but no fever at home. My outside labs showed high liver enzymes, so my specialists told me to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned a headache and fatigue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the headache started at the back of my neck and goes up. I’m also more tired than usual, though I’ve had baseline fatigue since my transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Any nausea, vomiting, or abdominal pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have chronic abdominal pain, mostly after eating. I take tramadol for it. No vomiting, but I haven’t had a bowel movement in three days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Okay, we’ll address that. We’ve drawn blood. Your white count is elevated, and your liver enzymes are quite high—AST and ALT over 400.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds bad. Could this be related to my liver transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’re concerned about cholangitis—an infection in the bile ducts. We’ve started blood cultures to check for bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cholangitis? I’ve heard of that. Is it serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can be, especially with your history. But we’re catching it early. We’ll start IV antibiotics as a precaution while we wait for results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your ultrasound showed chronic bile duct narrowing, which can trap bacteria. That supports the cholangitis concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So that’s why I keep having liver issues?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The narrowed ducts don’t drain well, increasing infection risk. We’ll need to clear that, but first, we treat the infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—the blood culture grew Citrobacter freundii, a gram-negative bacteria. It’s sensitive to meropenem, which you’re already on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that the right antibiotic? I’m allergic to penicillin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Meropenem is a carbapenem, not a penicillin, and safe for you. It’s very effective against this bug.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is up to 3.0. Nephrology thinks it’s from dehydration. They recommend more fluids by mouth.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been drinking, but not a lot. My appetite’s been off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll encourage you to drink more. Your kidney ultrasound showed no blockage, so that’s reassuring.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also checked for Lyme disease and CMV, given your symptoms. Both came back negative.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I was worried about Lyme since I hike sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good to rule it out. Your headache is likely from the infection, not Lyme.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are starting to come down—ALT is now 220, down from 392. That’s a good sign the antibiotics are working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What about the bile duct issue?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning an ERCP tomorrow. We’ll look inside the ducts and place a stent to help them drain better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that fix the problem?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should help prevent future infections. You’ll likely need another one in six months to check or replace it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The ERCP went well. We found strictures and placed a stent. No complications.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel better already. Any restrictions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just take it easy today. We’ll monitor you and plan your next steps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re also adjusting your sirolimus dose from 3 mg to 2 mg daily because of the infection. It’s an immunosuppressant, so we lower it during serious infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not long-term. We’ll check your level in a few weeks and may increase it back once you’re fully recovered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is down to 1.8—much better. Keep drinking fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been trying. I still feel a bit bloated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s common after the procedure. Your abdomen is soft and not tender now, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve placed a PICC line in your right arm. This will let you get IV antibiotics at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. You’ll finish a 14-day course of ertapenem through the PICC.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the stent? Will I feel it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You shouldn’t. It just keeps the duct open. We’ll check it in six months with another ERCP.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning look great. Liver enzymes are near normal, and your white count is down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my constipation?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep you on polyethylene glycol and senna. Stay hydrated and keep moving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my tramadol for pain?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, continue as needed. But avoid overuse. We’ll coordinate with your pain clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home today. A nurse will teach you about the PICC line and antibiotics.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I feel much better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Follow up with your hepatologist, and call if you develop fever, pain, or redness at the PICC site.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And I’ll keep drinking fluids for my kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. You’ve done well. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—should I restart my full sirolimus dose after antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, stay on 2 mg. Your hepatologist will check your level and decide when to increase it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Appreciate all the care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Our team is glad you’re feeling better. See you in follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

summary.summary_paragraph: A male patient with a history of liver transplant, chronic kidney disease, and GERD was admitted for chills and markedly elevated liver enzymes. He was found to have cholangitis due to Citrobacter freundii bacteremia, confirmed by blood cultures. He was started on meropenem, and an ERCP revealed bile duct strictures that were stented. His immunosuppressant sirolimus was reduced from 3 mg to 2 mg daily during the infection. Renal function, which was initially impaired with creatinine at 3.0, improved to 1.5 with oral hydration. Liver enzymes normalized significantly by discharge. A PICC line was placed for outpatient IV ertapenem to complete a 14-day course. He was discharged home in stable condition with plans for follow-up and a repeat ERCP in six months.
